{{Short description|Number system used by the Muisca}}
{{Muisca sidebar}}
{{Numeral systems}}
'''Muisca numerals''' were the numeric notation system used by the [[Muisca people|Muisca]], one of the civilizations of the [[Americas]] before the [[Spanish conquest of the Muisca]]. Just like the [[maya numerals|Mayas]], the Muisca had a [[vigesimal]] numerical system, based on multiples of twenty ([[Chibcha language|Chibcha]]: ''gueta''). The Muisca numerals were based on counting with fingers and toes. They had specific numbers from one to ten, yet for the numbers between eleven and nineteen they used "foot one" (11) to "foot nine" (19). The number 20 was the 'perfect' number for the Muisca which is visible in their [[Muisca calendar|calendar]]. To calculate higher numbers than 20 they used multiples of their 'perfect' number; ''gue-muyhica'' would be "20 times 4", so 80. To describe "50" they used "20 times 2 plus 10"; ''gue-bosa asaqui ubchihica'', transcribed from ''guêboʒhas aſaqɣ hubchìhicâ''.<ref name=Lugo>{{in lang|es}} 1619 - [http://www.cubun.org/desarrollos/numeros.php Muisca numbers according to Bernardo de Lugo] - accessed 29-04-2016</ref> In their [[Muisca calendar|calendar]], which was [[lunisolar]], they only counted from one to ten and twenty. Each number had a special meaning, related to their [[Muisca religion|deities]] and certain animals, especially the abundant [[toad]]s.<ref name=Izquierdo_p30>Izquierdo, 2009, p.30</ref>

For the representation of their numbers they used digits inspired by their natural surroundings, especially [[toad]]s; ''ata'' ("one") and ''aca'' ("nine") were both derived from the animals so abundant on the [[Bogotá savanna]] and other parts of the [[Altiplano Cundiboyacense]] where the Muisca lived in their [[Muisca Confederation|confederation]].

The most important scholars who provided knowledge about the Muisca numerals were [[Bernardo de Lugo]] (1619),<ref name=Lugo/> [[Pedro Simón]] (17th century), [[Alexander von Humboldt]] and [[José Domingo Duquesne]] (late 18th and 19th century) and [[Liborio Zerda]].<ref name=Humb1>Humboldt, 1878, Part 1</ref><ref name=Humb2>Humboldt, 1878, Part 2</ref><ref name=Humb3>Humboldt, 1878, Part 3</ref><ref name=Duquesne>Duquesne, 1795</ref><ref>Zerda, 1883</ref>

== Numerals ==
The Muisca used a vigesimal counting system and counted primarily with their fingers and secondarily with their toes. Their system went from 1 to 10 and for higher numerations they used the prefix ''quihicha'' or ''qhicha'', which means "foot" in their [[Chibcha language]] ''Muysccubun''. Eleven became thus "foot one", twelve: "foot two", etc. As in the other [[pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian]] civilizations, the number 20 was special. It was the total number of all body extremities; fingers and toes. The Muisca used two forms to express twenty: "foot ten"; ''quihícha ubchihica'' or their exclusive word ''gueta'', derived from ''gue'', which means "house". Numbers between 20 and 30 were counted ''gueta asaqui ata'' ("twenty plus one"; 21), ''gueta asaqui ubchihica'' ("twenty plus ten"; 30). Larger numbers were counted as multiples of twenty; ''gue-bosa'' ("20 times 2"; 40), ''gue-hisca'' ("20 times 5"; 100).<ref name=Humb1/>

[[File:Muisca cyphers acc acosta humboldt zerda.svg|right|thumb|260px|'''Muisca numerals''' as depicted by [[Joaquín Acosta|Acosta]], [[Alexander von Humboldt|Von Humboldt]] and [[Liborio Zerda|Zerda]]<ref name=Izquierdo_p43>Izquierdo Peña, 2009, p.43</ref>]] The numeral symbols were first provided by Duquesne and reproduced by Humboldt,<ref name=Humb1/> Acosta, and Zerda. These glyphs have been criticized and their authenticity questioned, as they are “practically nonexistent” in the surviving archaeological record, including the calendar stone from Choachí. Potentially, they might represent asterisms or months instead of numerals.<ref name=Izquierdo_p42-120>Izquierdo Peña, 2009, pp.42-44, 118-120</ref>
